title: SQL Day 8 — Multi-Table JOINs, Join Validation & Data Integrity
description: Combine related business tables safely and detect row multiplication, unmatched records, and grain problems.

topics.title: INNER JOIN
topics.business_skill: Combine records that have matching keys in both tables.

teaching.teacher: ## INNER JOIN\nINNER JOIN returns only rows with matching join keys on both sides.
teaching.explain: The ON clause defines how records relate; the selected columns define the business output.
teaching.detailedlearning: Before joining, identify the primary/foreign-key relationship and expected grain.
teaching.expose: A join is a data relationship, not merely a way to add columns.
teaching.example: SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
teaching.business_question: The manager wants order details with customer names.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name, o.sales FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

topics.title: Table Aliases & Qualified Columns
topics.business_skill: Write readable joins without ambiguous column references.

teaching.teacher: ## Aliases\nShort aliases such as o and c make multi-table SQL readable and prevent ambiguity.
teaching.explain: Qualify shared column names with their table alias.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use aliases consistently, especially when multiple tables contain order_id, customer_id, or region.
teaching.expose: Readable SQL is easier to audit and less likely to reference the wrong column.
teaching.example: SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
teaching.business_question: The senior analyst wants a clean customer-order query.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT o.order_id, o.sales, c.customer_name, c.segment FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

topics.title: LEFT JOIN & Unmatched Records
topics.business_skill: Preserve the primary table while identifying missing relationships.

teaching.teacher: ## LEFT JOIN\nLEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and adds matching data when available.
teaching.explain: It is ideal for completeness checks because unmatched right-side records produce NULLs.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use the left table as the population you must preserve.
teaching.expose: Moving a filter on the right table into WHERE can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
teaching.example: SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id=c.customer_id;
teaching.business_question: Data quality wants every order, including orders with no customer match.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, c.customer_name FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id=c.customer_id;

topics.title: Join Grain & Row Multiplication
topics.business_skill: Detect duplicate metrics caused by one-to-many joins.

teaching.teacher: ## Join grain\nJoining tables at incompatible grains can multiply rows and inflate SUM or COUNT results.
teaching.explain: Always ask how many rows can match each row on the other side.
teaching.detailedlearning: Validate row counts before and after joins and compare expected keys.
teaching.expose: A query can run successfully while producing incorrect KPIs.
teaching.example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id=c.customer_id;
teaching.business_question: The analyst suspects a join has inflated sales.
teaching.expected_sql: Compare row counts and sales before and after the join, grouped at the expected grain.

topics.title: Validated Multi-Table KPI
topics.business_skill: Build a joined KPI only after validating relationships.

teaching.teacher: ## Join validation\nA production KPI should include relationship checks before aggregation.
teaching.explain: Validate key uniqueness, unmatched rates, and row counts before trusting joined totals.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use separate validation queries or CTE layers to make assumptions explicit.
teaching.expose: Correct joins are part of KPI governance.
teaching.example: SELECT c.segment, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders, SUM(o.sales) AS sales FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id=c.customer_id GROUP BY c.segment;
teaching.business_question: The customer director wants segment-level order and sales KPIs.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT c.segment, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders, SUM(o.sales) AS sales FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id=c.customer_id GROUP BY c.segment;
